  "chapter_body_excerpt": "# 6 Replenish or attack? Competing etiologies and therapies of madness in Ming medicine When there is depletion, replenish it; when there is repletion: drain it. 虛者補之 實者瀉之 Canon of Problems 難經, problem 69 This chapter explains the rich developments that took place in elite medical thinking and practice from roughly 1530 to 1650. In addition to writing long sections on diankuang in their treatises, physicians from this ebullient period recorded in some detail how they handled specific cases of madness. All of these men had read the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法 (1482), knew of Wang Lun's 王綸 (1453-1510) arguments on Yin-replenishing, and embraced a syncretistic approach to past medical teachings. Their clinical practice and most of the doctrinal debates in which they engaged were thus informed by the trends in medical thinking that I described in previous chapters. In the domain that interests us, the main event of the sixteenth century was perhaps the re-definition of dian 癲 as a form of madness characterized by non-manic symptoms and best treated by replenishing. The illness dian had existed since at least the third century BCE, and it had been associated with kuang since the first century BCE, but its main symptoms had first been close to those of epilepsy. When dian had been re-interpreted as a form of madness in the twelfth century, it had become so close to kuang in both etiology and symptoms that it could hardly be differentiated from kuang (3.4, 4.1). Dissatisfied with this confusion, many sixteenth-century physicians tried to reassert differences between dian and kuang. The clarifications proposed by a physician from Huizhou called Sun Yikui 孫一奎 (1522-1619) were eventually accepted by most elite physicians in the following centuries.
